source.name: usp_UpdateInventory

result.generatedDdl:
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE dbo.usp_UpdateInventory(
    p_ProductID INT,
    p_NewQuantity INT
)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    -- SET NOCOUNT ON equivalent: PostgreSQL doesn't send row counts by default in procedures
    
    UPDATE dbo.Products p
    SET StockQuantity = p_NewQuantity
    WHERE p.ProductID = p_ProductID
    FOR UPDATE; -- Equivalent to UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK
    
END;
$$;
assumptions: The schema 'dbo' exists in PostgreSQL or will be created
The Products table exists with columns ProductID (INT) and StockQuantity (INT)
Parameter naming convention changed from @ParamName to p_ParamName to follow PostgreSQL best practices
SET NOCOUNT ON is not needed in PostgreSQL as procedures don't return row counts by default
FOR UPDATE clause provides row-level locking similar to UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK hints
No explicit transaction control needed as the procedure will run in the caller's transaction context

reviewFlags.reason: SQL Server's WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) and PostgreSQL's FOR UPDATE have subtle differences. UPDLOCK prevents other transactions from acquiring update locks, while FOR UPDATE locks rows for update. The locking behavior may differ under high concurrency. Consider if SELECT...FOR UPDATE should be used separately before the UPDATE.

The UPDATE statement in PostgreSQL doesn't support table hints. The FOR UPDATE clause is placed at the end, but this syntax is typically used with SELECT statements. In an UPDATE statement, PostgreSQL automatically locks the rows being updated. Verify if additional locking strategy is needed.

compatibilityNotes.description: SQL Server's UPDLOCK and ROWLOCK hints provide explicit control over lock granularity and type. PostgreSQL's UPDATE statement automatically acquires row-level locks (FOR UPDATE semantics). The FOR UPDATE clause shown is typically used in SELECT statements. PostgreSQL UPDATE statements inherently lock rows being modified, which may be sufficient for most use cases.

The locking behavior may vary depending on the transaction isolation level. SQL Server defaults to READ COMMITTED with row versioning in newer versions, while PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED without MVCC-based snapshot isolation for updates. Consider setting appropriate isolation levels at the session or transaction level.
PostgreSQL procedures do not return row count messages by default, so SET NOCOUNT ON has no direct equivalent and is omitted.
